1.o: In this chapter we have, I. The proclamation which Cyrus, king of Persia, issued out for the release of all the Jews that he found captives in Babylon, and the building of their temple in Jerusalem, ver. 1-4. II. The return of many thereupon, ver. 5, 6. III. Orders given for the restoring of the vessels of the temple, ver. 7-11. And this is the dawning of the day of their deliverance.
1.i: King Cyrus lets the Jewish exiles go home to Jerusalem and gives back the temple treasures.
1.p: Lord, You bring Your people home. Thank You for keeping Your promises, even after seventy years. Amen.
1.l: Welcome someone who is new in your school or neighborhood and help them feel at home.
q: God stirred the heart of a foreign king. Whose heart might God stir to help you?

2.o: That many returned out of Babylon upon Cyrus's proclamation we were told in the foregoing chapter; we have here a catalogue of the several families that returned, ver. 1. I. The leaders, ver. 2. II. The people, ver. 3-35. III. The priests, Levites, and retainers to the temple, ver. 35-63. IV. The sum total, with an account of their retinue, ver. 64-67. V. Their offerings to the service of the temple, ver. 68-70.

3.o: In the close of the foregoing chapter we left Israel in their cities, but we may well imagine what a bad posture their affairs were in, the ground untilled, the cities in ruins, all out of order; but here we have an account of the early care they took about the re-establishment of religion among them. Thus did they lay the foundation well, and begin their work at the right end. I. They set up an altar, and offered sacrifices upon it, kept the feasts, and contributed towards the rebuilding of the temple, ver. 1-7.
3.i: The foundation of the new temple is laid, and the people shout for joy while the old priests weep.
3.p: Lord, You are good, and Your love lasts forever. Help us to make room for both joy and tears. Amen.
3.l: Be gentle today with someone who is sad when others are happy, and listen to them.
q: The same foundation made some people laugh and others cry. How do you respond to change?

4.o: The good work of rebuilding the temple was no sooner begun than it met with opposition from those that bore ill will to it; the Samaritans were enemies to the Jews and their religion, and they set themselves to obstruct it. I. They offered to be partners in the building of it, that they might have it in their power to retard it; but they were refused, ver. 1-3. II. They discouraged them in it, and dissuaded them from it, ver. 4, 5. III.
4.i: Ezra 4 to 6 recount a project nearly killed by opposition, delay, and letters, and finished by prophecy and a paper in an archive.
4.p: Lord, You turn the hearts of kings. Give us courage to keep building, and joy when the work is done. Amen.
4.l: When something you are working on gets stopped, ask God what He wants you to do next, and keep going.
q: The neighbors were taught to worship a god of the land while keeping their own gods. What do you add to your faith that was never part of it?

5.o: We left the temple-work at a full stop; but, being God's work, it shall be revived, and here we have an account of the reviving of it. It was hindered by might and power, but it was set a-going again "by the Spirit of the Lord of hosts." Now here we are told how that blessed Spirit, I. Warmed its cool-hearted friends and excited them to build, ver. 1, 2. II.
5.i: Ezra 4 to 6 recount a project nearly killed by opposition, delay, and letters, and finished by prophecy and a paper in an archive.
5.p: Lord, You turn the hearts of kings. Give us courage to keep building, and joy when the work is done. Amen.
5.l: When something you are working on gets stopped, ask God what He wants you to do next, and keep going.
q: The neighbors were taught to worship a god of the land while keeping their own gods. What do you add to your faith that was never part of it?

6.o: How solemnly the foundation of the temple was laid we read in ch. iii. How slowly the building went on, and with how much difficulty, we found in ch. iv. and v. But how gloriously the topstone was at length brought forth with shoutings we find in this chapter; and even we, at this distance of time, when we read of it, may cry, "Grace, grace to it." As for God, his work is perfect; it may be slow work, but it will be sure work. We have here, I. A recital of the decree of Cyrus for the building of the temple, ver.
6.i: Ezra 4 to 6 recount a project nearly killed by opposition, delay, and letters, and finished by prophecy and a paper in an archive.
6.p: Lord, You turn the hearts of kings. Give us courage to keep building, and joy when the work is done. Amen.
6.l: When something you are working on gets stopped, ask God what He wants you to do next, and keep going.
q: The neighbors were taught to worship a god of the land while keeping their own gods. What do you add to your faith that was never part of it?

7.o: Ezra's precious name saluted us, at first, in the title of the book, but in the history we have not met with it till this chapter introduces him into public action in another reign, that of Artaxerxes. Zerubbabel and Jeshua we will suppose, by this time, to have grown old, if not gone off; nor do we hear any more of Haggai and Zechariah; they have finished their testimony. What shall become of the cause of God and Israel when these useful instruments are laid aside?
7.s: A Fast by the Ahava Canal
7.i: Ezra leads a second group of exiles from Babylon to Jerusalem, and before they go, they fast and pray for protection.
7.p: Lord, You are our protector on every road. Teach us to ask for Your help, and to be faithful to what we say we believe. Amen.
7.l: Before you start a trip or a big job, stop and ask God to go with you.
q: Ezra felt he should rely on God rather than soldiers. What do you rely on?

8.o: This chapter gives us a more particular narrative of Ezra's journey to Jerusalem, of which we had a general account in the foregoing chapter I. The company that went up with him, ver. 1-20. II. The solemn fast which he kept with his company, to implore God's presence with them in this journey, ver. 21-23. III. The care he took of the treasure he had with him, and the charge he gave concerning it to the priests, to whose custody he committed it, ver. 24-30. IV.
8.s: A Fast by the Ahava Canal
8.i: Ezra leads a second group of exiles from Babylon to Jerusalem, and before they go, they fast and pray for protection.
8.p: Lord, You are our protector on every road. Teach us to ask for Your help, and to be faithful to what we say we believe. Amen.
8.l: Before you start a trip or a big job, stop and ask God to go with you.
q: Ezra felt he should rely on God rather than soldiers. What do you rely on?

9.o: The affairs of the church were in a very good posture, we may well suppose, now that Ezra presided in them. Look without; the government was kind to them. We hear no complaints of persecution and oppression; their enemies had either their hearts turned or at least their hands tied; their neighbours were civil, and we hear of no wars nor rumours of wars; there were none to make them afraid; all was as well as could be, considering that they were few, and poor, and subjects to a foreign prince.
9.i: Ezra 9 and 10 are among the hardest chapters in the book: a prayer of deep shame, and a painful decision about marriages.
9.p: Lord, we are ashamed of our sins and we need Your mercy. Give us honest tears and hearts that turn. Amen.
9.l: Say sorry to God today for one specific thing, using your own words, not a ready-made prayer.
q: Weeping is good but reforming is better. What have you grieved over that you have not yet changed?

10.o: In this chapter we have that grievance redressed which was complained of and lamented in the foregoing chapter. Observe, I. How the people's hearts were prepared for the redress of it by their deep humiliation for the sin, ver. 1. II. How it was proposed to Ezra by Shechaniah, ver. 2-4. III. How the proposal was put in execution. 1. The great men were sworn to stand to it, ver. 5. 2. Ezra appeared first in it, ver. 6. 3. A general assembly was called, ver. 7-9. 4.
10.i: Ezra 9 and 10 are among the hardest chapters in the book: a prayer of deep shame, and a painful decision about marriages.

10.l: Say sorry to God today for one specific thing, using your own words, not a ready-made prayer.
